section_summary: This section documents State Department concern over Japanese propaganda and suspected intelligence activities in the United States during 1938–1939, including consular distribution of pamphlets, photography of transportation infrastructure, possession of Grand Coulee Dam plans, and reports from the Colorado River Delta. It also contains allegations of German-Japanese intelligence cooperation, propaganda directed at African Americans, and several cross-references to suspected agents. The final group concerns Japanese Army surgeon Ryoichi Naito’s unsuccessful effort to obtain yellow-fever virus from the Rockefeller Institute and the attempted bribery of an institute technician.

subfiles.title: Evaluation of Japanese propaganda material distributed in the United States
subfiles.about: Evaluates pamphlets, newspapers, and handbills allegedly distributed through Japanese official channels.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum characterizes several items as overt or disguised paid Japanese propaganda and distinguishes them from independent American opinion. It identifies the Pamphleteer, the California Committee of Pacific Friendship, the Japanese-American Publishing Company, and the Society for Promotion of Pacific Peace, while noting that little information was available about several of them. It also cites Consul Mazutani's Chicago speech blaming outside sympathy and the Brussels Conference for prolonging the war in China.

subfiles.title: Report on publishers of Japanese propaganda material
subfiles.from: Harley Notter, Division of Research and Publication
subfiles.about: Reports the results of research into organizations publishing material favorable to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Notter states that the findings are largely negative because several publishing groups were too new to appear in available studies. He supplies addresses and background for the Pamphleteer, the California Committee of Pacific Friendship, the Japanese-American Publishing Company, and the Society for Promotion of Pacific Peace. He finds the Japanese-American reputable but directed mainly at Japanese residents and cannot determine the backing of the other groups.

subfiles.title: Disposition of Japanese propaganda papers
subfiles.about: Suggests disposing of the propaganda papers while transferring the departmental portion to records custody.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck recommends that McDermott dispose of the papers. He suggests that the departmental portion might instead be sent to the Division of Communications and Records.

subfiles.title: Foreign-government propaganda in the United States
subfiles.to: Sumner Welles and the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Raises the broader policy question of regulating propaganda conducted in the United States for foreign governments.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck calls attention to printed propaganda reportedly distributed by the Japanese Consulate General in Chicago and suggests that Japanese official agencies are distributing similar material on a large scale. He asks whether foreign-government propaganda should continue unchecked when American consultants and public agents prepare unattributed material for editorialists, lecturers, and officials. The memorandum urges serious consideration of regulation without proposing an immediate measure.

subfiles.title: Internal review of the Chicago propaganda case
subfiles.about: Explains disagreement within the Far Eastern Division over how the Department should respond to Japanese propaganda.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton transmits documents concerning propaganda material obtained from the Japanese Consulate in Chicago and apologizes for delay caused by disagreements among Far Eastern Division officers. He agrees generally with Ballantine and Vincent that a stronger government position may eventually be required. He doubts the value of approaching the Japanese Embassy unless the Department expects cooperation or is prepared to carry the matter further.

subfiles.title: Recommended response to Japanese consular propaganda
subfiles.from: Joseph W. Ballantine and John Carter Vincent
subfiles.about: Assesses Japanese propaganda publications and proposes an informal warning to the Japanese Embassy.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum finds that the material plainly seeks to present Japanese actions in China favorably but is not subversive or generally derogatory toward American institutions. Its American and Japanese publishers appear entitled to issue or import it, and the evidence does not establish that the Chicago consul was actively distributing it beyond supplying callers. The authors advise against official action but suggest informally asking the Japanese Embassy counselor to discourage consular propaganda activity.

subfiles.title: Summary of Paris report on German-Japanese intelligence cooperation
subfiles.about: Summarizes a Paris despatch alleging cooperation between German and Japanese intelligence services.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum notes that Paris despatch no. 2376 contains information from a Soviet Embassy secretary. The source alleged that German and Japanese intelligence services exchanged information and sometimes conducted large-scale espionage for each other.

subfiles.title: Despatch no. 2376: Japanese and German espionage
subfiles.from: Maynard B. Barnes, U.S. Embassy, Paris
subfiles.about: Transmits an embassy memorandum concerning alleged German-Japanese espionage cooperation.
subfiles.summary: Barnes forwards a confidential memorandum prepared from information supplied by the First Secretary of the Soviet Embassy in Paris. The enclosure concerns cooperation between Japanese and German espionage services.

subfiles.title: Memorandum for the Ambassador on Japanese and German espionage
subfiles.about: Reports Birukov's allegations that German and Japanese intelligence services conducted operations for one another.
subfiles.summary: Birukov claimed that the withdrawal of the German Military Mission from China would give Japan access to valuable information about Chinese forces. He alleged close German-Japanese intelligence cooperation and suggested that German espionage under investigation in the United States had been conducted for Japan because German and German-American agents attracted less attention. Higgins cautioned that the claim might be fantastic but considered it useful as evidence of Soviet intelligence views.

subfiles.title: Society of American Military Engineers transmittal letter
subfiles.from: M. K. Lutz, Society of American Military Engineers
subfiles.about: Forwards C. H. Weeks's report of Japanese photography in the Sierra Nevada.
subfiles.summary: Lutz encloses a self-explanatory letter for the Department's information and any use it considers appropriate. He states that the enclosure is being transmitted at the author's request.

subfiles.title: Report of Japanese photography of California transportation routes
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese individuals photographing and taking notes on railroads, highways, and bridges across the Sierra Nevada.
subfiles.summary: Weeks states that he saw occupants of two automobiles photographing critical transportation points over the Sierra Nevada summit and taking notes. He says that he had observed similar activity openly on several occasions during the preceding two years. He asks that military authorities be informed so they may act as their judgment directs.

subfiles.title: Referral of the Weeks report to the Attorney General
subfiles.about: Forwards the Weeks correspondence for consideration by the Department of Justice.
subfiles.summary: The Secretary of State encloses the military engineers' letter and C. H. Weeks's report concerning Japanese activities in California. The note says copies were also sent to the Secretaries of War and the Navy and that the originating society was informed of the referrals.

subfiles.title: Referral of the Weeks report to the Secretary of the Navy
subfiles.about: Forwards the Weeks report of Japanese photography for naval consideration.
subfiles.summary: The State Department sends the Navy copies of the Society of American Military Engineers' letter and Weeks's enclosure. It notes parallel referrals to the Secretary of War and the Attorney General.

subfiles.title: Referral of the Weeks report to the Secretary of War
subfiles.about: Forwards the Weeks report of Japanese photography for War Department consideration.
subfiles.summary: The State Department provides the War Department with the military engineers' letter and Weeks's report. The note records that the Navy and Justice Departments received copies as well.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to M. K. Lutz
subfiles.from: Joseph W. Ballantine, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the report and states that it was sent to appropriate government authorities.
subfiles.summary: Ballantine thanks Lutz for forwarding Weeks's report about Japanese activities in the California mountains. He says the correspondence has been brought to the attention of the appropriate authorities.

subfiles.title: Navy acknowledgment of the Weeks correspondence
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the State Department's referral concerning C. H. Weeks's report.
subfiles.summary: The Navy acknowledges the July 25 State Department letter and its copy of the Society of American Military Engineers' correspondence. The note identifies Weeks and Truckee, California, but gives no further assessment.

subfiles.title: Justice Department acknowledgment of the Weeks correspondence
subfiles.from: Brian McMahon, for the Attorney General
subfiles.about: Acknowledges information about unidentified Japanese photographing California railroads, highways, and bridges.
subfiles.summary: The Justice Department confirms receipt of the State Department's July 25 communication and enclosures. It notes that the same matter had been brought to the attention of the Secretaries of War and the Navy.

subfiles.title: Anonymous warning about Japanese military reconnaissance
subfiles.to: Department of State or another federal official
subfiles.about: Warns of purported Japanese reconnaissance and argues for stronger treatment of suspected foreign operatives.
subfiles.summary: The poorly legible letter refers to reports of Japanese officers being arrested while photographing or possessing maps near American military or strategic locations, including Charlestown and San Diego. The writer argues that such activities form part of a continuing pattern and urges that the information be sent to an appropriate official. The conclusion contrasts American tolerance with Japan's presumed harsh response to comparable conduct by Americans.

subfiles.title: Tokyo rejects U.S. protest over attack on airliner
subfiles.about: Reports Japan's rejection of an American protest over the machine-gunning of a Chinese-American airliner.
subfiles.summary: The Japanese government rejected every count of the American protest over the August 24 destruction of an airliner near Canton. Its reply nevertheless admitted that Japanese aircraft continued attacking after the airliner landed on a river between Canton and Macau.

subfiles.title: FBI report on Japanese possession of Grand Coulee Dam drawings
subfiles.from: John Edgar Hoover, Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Reports that the Japanese Consulate in Seattle possessed Grand Coulee Dam construction drawings and sought multiple blueprint copies.
subfiles.summary: Hoover states that a confidential source learned that the Seattle Japanese Consulate had drawings showing the construction of Grand Coulee Dam and wanted twenty-one blueprint copies of each. The FBI obtained seven blueprints and sent photostatic copies to the State Department. Naval Intelligence director R. S. Holmes had also been informed.

subfiles.title: Grand Coulee Dam engineering drawings
subfiles.about: Provides duplicated engineering diagrams and maps of Grand Coulee Dam, its power and pumping system, geology, and cofferdams.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure contains plans for river diversion, a diagram of the proposed power and pumping plant, damsite topography, a geological cross-section, structural sections, cofferdam sections, and regional maps. Several sheets contain Japanese annotations, and the sequence of drawings is substantially duplicated. These are the drawings obtained in connection with the FBI report about the Seattle Japanese Consulate.

subfiles.title: State Department reply concerning the Grand Coulee drawings
subfiles.from: R. Walton Moore, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the FBI's Grand Coulee report and suggests informing Army intelligence.
subfiles.summary: Moore thanks the FBI for reporting that the Seattle Japanese Consulate possessed Grand Coulee construction drawings and for supplying blueprint copies. He notes that Naval Intelligence had already been apprised and suggests that the Military Intelligence Division of the War Department also be notified.

subfiles.title: War Department Intelligence Division routing sheet
subfiles.about: Routes the attached confidential report on Japanese activities in the Colorado River Delta.
subfiles.summary: The sheet lists War Department, service-branch, Naval Intelligence, State Department, Commerce Department, and corps-area recipients. It accompanies the report concerning Japanese residents and infrastructure activity near the Colorado River Delta.

subfiles.title: Japanese activities in the Colorado River Delta area
subfiles.to: William W. Lloyd, Intelligence Officer, Fort Huachuca
subfiles.about: Reports on Japanese residents, farming, fishing, railway construction, canals, and harbor surveys in the Mexican Colorado River Delta.
subfiles.summary: Kneeland reports that no Japanese engineers were known to have assisted the railway extension from Mexicali toward El Golfo and Rocky Point, but identifies several Japanese families living south of San Luis. He describes Frank Kans, Louis Katsurayama, N. Nakaoka, and Pedro Wakamatsu, including their language skills, occupations, finances, and possible military background. The report also mentions a Japanese canal contractor, resumed railway and irrigation work, and preliminary harbor surveys at El Golfo.

subfiles.title: Report of a Japanese fleet near Vancouver Island
subfiles.about: Passes on an unverified report that a Japanese fleet was sighted about 250 miles off Vancouver Island.
subfiles.summary: Willcox says that a seemingly trustworthy informant had heard from an officer who passed a Japanese fleet offshore. He offers to investigate in Vancouver, Seattle, Tacoma, Portland, or San Francisco and to interrupt planned travel if the president wishes. He speculates about Vancouver Island's strategic value as a fortress and air base.

subfiles.title: Follow-up on the Vancouver Island fleet rumor
subfiles.about: Reports further investigation of the alleged Japanese squadron sighting and discusses European and Pacific war dangers.
subfiles.summary: Willcox says the intelligence staff at Esquimalt had not received the report and that a newspaper office pronounced it unfounded, though he remained suspicious. He proposes identifying the vessel and contacting its officers through his informant. The letter expands into warnings about Hong Kong, British leadership, German air strength, Charles Lindbergh, and Frederick Schuman's claim that the recent war scare was manufactured.

subfiles.title: Japanese propaganda directed at Pittsburgh's African American population
subfiles.about: Forwards a newspaper story about a Japanese-sponsored migration offer to African Americans and warns of local propaganda effects.
subfiles.summary: McKee encloses a page from the Pittsburgh Courier describing what he calls a preposterous offer by a Japanese professor on behalf of the Japanese government. He states that Japanese propaganda, official entertainment, and goodwill tourists are having a serious effect on Pittsburgh's African American population.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Frederick C. McKee
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges McKee's letter and Pittsburgh Courier enclosure.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton confirms receipt of McKee's November 21 letter and the October 29 newspaper page. He says the material was read with interest and thanks McKee for bringing it to the Department's attention.

subfiles.title: Reader's Digest transmittal of Japanese propaganda material
subfiles.about: Forwards another copy of the Japanese propaganda item previously sent to the Secretary of State.
subfiles.summary: Littell suggests adding the enclosed item to Hornbeck's collection of Japanese propaganda. He notes that Frederick C. McKee's covering letter indicates that the Secretary had already received a copy.

subfiles.title: McKee letter to Robert Littell
subfiles.about: Sends Littell a copy of Japanese propaganda previously forwarded to Secretary Hull.
subfiles.summary: McKee congratulates Littell on an article about cigarette holders. He encloses what he describes as recent Japanese propaganda and notes that he also sent it to Secretary Hull.

subfiles.title: Pittsburgh Courier article on a Japanese back-to-Africa proposal
subfiles.about: Reports Itake Coo's offer of Japanese-supported transportation, land, and supplies for three million African Americans to settle in Africa.
subfiles.summary: The article says Itake Coo offered free passage from Los Angeles, seventy-five acres, a house, equipment, animals, and seed under alleged Japanese government sponsorship. Coo could not identify the land beyond saying it would be near the Gold Coast, although Japan controlled no African territory. He urged African Americans to organize under Japanese guidance, invoked Lothrop Stoddard, and portrayed Japan as destined to lead the world's nonwhite peoples against whites.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck acknowledgment to Robert Littell
subfiles.about: Thanks Littell for his letter and propaganda enclosure.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck thanks Littell for the thoughtful courtesy of sending his December 21 letter and its enclosure. He closes with seasonal good wishes.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Milan report on Japanese secret-service activity
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to another file containing further information on Japanese secret-service activity in the United States and South America.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers to file 862.20211/1895. The referenced document concerns Japanese secret-service activities in the United States and South America and records the receipt of additional information.

subfiles.title: Internal comment on secret-service information
subfiles.about: Records a brief, largely illegible internal reaction to intelligence concerning Japanese secret-service activities.
subfiles.summary: The handwritten notation evaluates information routed to the Division of Far Eastern Affairs. Much of the text is illegible, but it appears to comment on the information's significance and possible discussion or handling.

subfiles.title: Post Office transmittal concerning suspected spy Kenzie
subfiles.from: K. P. Aldrich, Chief Inspector, Post Office Department
subfiles.about: Forwards a postal inspector's report alleging that a Pueblo industrial worker might be a Japanese spy.
subfiles.summary: Aldrich transmits J. A. Willey's December 31 report about Kenzie, an employee of the Colorado Fuel and Iron Corporation. He submits the matter to Dunn for whatever attention the State Department considers appropriate.

subfiles.title: Report of suspicion that Kenzie was a Japanese spy
subfiles.from: J. A. Willey, Post Office Inspector
subfiles.about: Records a rumor that Colorado Fuel and Iron employee Kenzie served the Japanese government.
subfiles.summary: Postmaster Charles F. Horn told Willey that Joe Smith suspected Kenzie of being a Japanese spy. Kenzie had worked for the steel company for years and was regarded as a good and efficient workman, but allegedly said too much while intoxicated. Willey forwards the unverified rumor for any reference deemed advisable.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of the Kenzie report
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the Post Office report concerning Kenzie.
subfiles.summary: Dunn confirms receipt of Aldrich's January 9 letter and J. A. Willey's report. He thanks Aldrich for the information concerning Kenzie.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Harbin report on Sonoshichi Sueoka
subfiles.about: Refers to a despatch concerning an encounter with Japanese Army translator Sonoshichi Sueoka at Hailar.
subfiles.summary: The referenced despatch describes a conversation with Sonoshichi Sueoka, an Army translator attached to a Japanese detachment at Hailar. It suggests that Sueoka may have been sent by the military mission or gendarmerie to test whether Consul Benninghoff would respond to an offer of military secrets.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to allegations against Wiedemann and Hohenlohe
subfiles.about: Points to a Justice Department letter alleging espionage for Japan by Fritz Wiedemann and Princess Stephanie Hohenlohe.
subfiles.summary: The sheet refers researchers to file 702.6211/953. The referenced letter reportedly advises that Fritz Wiedemann and Princess Stephanie Hohenlohe were engaged in espionage activities for the Japanese government.

subfiles.title: Recommendation to close the pending espionage file
subfiles.to: Maxwell M. Hamilton and George S. Messersmith
subfiles.about: Recommends taking no action beyond securing the file and remembering the case.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck states that he sees no advantageous action that the Department can take in the case. He recommends locking up the file and keeping the matter in mind, while offering to explain his reasoning in conference.

subfiles.title: Verification of Ryoichi Naito's Japanese Army status
subfiles.about: Confirms from the Japanese Official Register that Ryoichi Naito was an Army medical officer assigned to the Army Medical College.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum identifies Naito as a second-class military surgeon assigned to the Army Medical College in Tokyo. This corroborates information in the Japanese military attaché's February 22 letter to Dr. Bauer. The Visa Division had requested Naito's visa record from the Labor Department.

subfiles.title: Confidential memorandum on the attempt to obtain yellow-fever virus
subfiles.to: Secretary and Under Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Reports Ryoichi Naito's requests for yellow-fever virus and an attempted bribe of a Rockefeller Institute employee.
subfiles.summary: Raymond Fosdick and Chauncey Belknap reported that the Rockefeller Institute had refused repeated efforts by Japanese Army surgeon Ryoichi Naito and military attaché Colonel Yamauti to secure access to its bacteriological work and a vial of yellow-fever virus. Soon after the refusal, an unknown man offered an institute employee as much as $3,000 to steal a vial, but the employee refused and informed his superiors. Institute scientists noted the absence of yellow fever and its mosquito vector in Japan but feared that the virus could cause a devastating outbreak in China. State Department officers considered searching Naito before his departure from San Francisco but rejected the idea as unlikely to produce evidence and likely to alert the Japanese.

subfiles.title: Trans-Pacific steamship departure list
subfiles.about: Lists possible March sailings for Naito's return journey to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The note lists the Chichibu Maru from San Francisco on March 2, the Hikawa Maru from Seattle on March 7, and the Empress of Asia from Vancouver on March 4. It appears to support consideration of Naito's intended departure.

subfiles.title: Ryoichi Naito identification cards
subfiles.to: Rockefeller Institute or Department of State file
subfiles.about: Displays cards identifying Naito as an assistant professor at the Japanese Army Medical College and as a Japanese staff physician in Berlin.
subfiles.summary: The page reproduces Naito's name and professional identification in English and German. It identifies him with the Army Medical College in Tokyo and gives a Wittelsbacherstrasse address associated with his stay in Berlin.

subfiles.title: Statement of Vladimir Glasounoff
subfiles.from: Vladimir Glasounoff, questioned by Chauncey Belknap
subfiles.about: Begins the sworn-style interview of the technician approached in connection with the attempt to obtain yellow-fever virus.
subfiles.summary: Glasounoff explains his duties caring for experimental mice and his authorized access to locked yellow-fever virus stores. The interview then establishes his background: birth and education in Moscow, naval service during the Russian Revolution, forced Red Army service, escape through Odesa and the Black Sea to Constantinople, later maritime work, and immigration to the United States with Mrs. Bristol's assistance in 1923. The transcript continues through his early employment history in New York and is incomplete at the end of this section.
